title: Harriet Tubman Leads the Combahee River Raid
text:
Harriet Tubman had escaped slavery in Maryland in 1849 and then returned again and again to guide others north. During the Civil War she went to the Union-held coast of South Carolina, where she worked as a nurse and organized a network of scouts among formerly enslaved people who knew the rivers and plantations of the area.

In the night of June 1 to 2, 1863, three Union gunboats carrying black soldiers of the 2nd South Carolina Volunteers, under Colonel James Montgomery, steamed up the Combahee River. Tubman went with them as a guide. Her scouts had located where Confederate mines lay in the river and where the troops were posted.

The soldiers landed, burned plantations and rice mills, and destroyed a pontoon bridge. When the boat whistles blew, enslaved people came running from the fields toward the river, carrying children, pots and animals. More than seven hundred were taken aboard and freed. Many of the men later joined the Union army.

Newspapers reported the raid and noted the role of a black woman. Tubman later spent decades petitioning the government for a pension for her wartime service.
lesson: Knowledge of the ground and the trust of the people on it can matter more than rank. Lead from what you know best.
source: Union army reports; Wisconsin State Journal and Commonwealth reports, 1863; Sarah Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869)
